framework.name: The Biblical Covenants (Concise Theology)
framework.author: Paul R. Williamson
framework.attribution: Covenant structure, chronology and key passages follow Paul R. Williamson, "The Biblical Covenants," The Gospel Coalition (Concise Theology), CC BY-SA 4.0, https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/the-biblical-covenants/.
framework.summary: The covenants form the unifying thread of God's saving action, beginning explicitly with Noah and reaching fulfilment in the new covenant ratified through the blood of Jesus Christ. The first explicit covenant in Scripture is Noah's; Abraham's follows; Moses continues God's dealings with Israel as a witness nation; David identifies the promised seed as a royal descendant of Abraham; Jesus ratifies the new covenant.
caveats: The essay counts only covenants that Scripture itself describes, so its first explicit covenant is Noah's. `cv_creation` is retained as a theological prior rather than an explicit covenant: the essay calls it a probationary "covenant of works/creation" belonging to Reformed/Covenant Theology, and records that other scholars are "unpersuaded" by it.
The essay argues for two Abrahamic covenants, kept here under the single `cv_abrahamic` id so no topic loses its tag. See `stages` on that covenant.

The Davidic covenant is never called one in its own establishing text. 2 Sam 7 and 1 Chr 17 promise a dynasty without using the word; the covenant framing comes from 2 Sam 23:5, 2 Chr 7:18, 2 Chr 13:5, Ps 89:3 and Jer 33:21.

A topic's covenant records the stage its primary text belongs to under this chronology. It is an editorial proposal, not a reviewed judgement: of the 1,140 assigned topics, 50 rest on a single cited verse, 126 on a cited chapter range, and 964 on a book-wide default.

covenants.name: Creation (Adam)
covenants.description: God's arrangement with Adam in the garden: a probationary covenant of works, per the framework essay's summary of Reformed/Covenant Theology. It is not an explicit covenant in Scripture; the word "covenant" does not appear in Genesis 1-3, which is why the essay records that other scholars are unpersuaded by it.

covenants.name: Noah
covenants.description: The first covenant Scripture itself describes. The word first appears at Gen 6:18; the covenant is established after the flood with the rainbow as its sign, promising that the natural order will never again be interrupted and that human life will be preserved on earth.

covenants.name: Abraham
covenants.description: God's covenants with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, which the framework essay argues are two rather than one: stage 1 ratifies the national promise of a great nation, stage 2 the international promise that Abraham's seed will mediate blessing to all peoples. Circumcision is the sign, and Abraham's obedience in Genesis 22 prompts God to ratify the promises by solemn oath.

stages.name: Abrahamic, stage 1: the national promise
stages.summary: God's promise to make Abram a great nation and to give him a great name. The essay treats Genesis 15:18 as the covenant ratifying this dimension, with offspring as the means of working out God's creative goal.
essayQuotes: the national dimension of God's promise is the focus of Genesis 15

stages.name: Abrahamic, stage 2: the international promise
stages.summary: The promise that through Abraham's seed all peoples on earth are blessed. Genesis 17 stresses nations, kings and a perpetual relationship with Abraham's seed, names Isaac as the one through whom it continues, and Genesis 22 ratifies it by solemn oath.
essayQuotes: God announces an "everlasting covenant" (17:7), the so-called "covenant of circumcision" (Acts 7:8)
Abraham's obedient faith (22:16,18) met the demands of 17:1... thus prompting God to ratify the promises of Genesis 17 by a solemn oath
two distinct covenants were established between God and Abraham

covenants.name: Moses (Sinai)
covenants.description: God's covenant at Sinai, which continues his dealings with the descendants of Abraham. Its focus is less on what Israel must do to inherit the land than on how it must live in the land as God's chosen people, so that the nations see God's holiness and wisdom. Sacrificial worship, especially the Day of Atonement, maintains the relationship when Israel rebels, and the same obligations are re-issued after the golden calf as an act of grace rather than justice.

covenants.name: David
covenants.description: Nathan's oracle to David: David intends to build a house for God, and God promises to build a house, a dynasty, for David. Neither 2 Samuel 7 nor 1 Chronicles 17 calls this a covenant, so the framing comes from 2 Samuel 23:5, 2 Chronicles 7:18 and 13:5, Psalm 89:3 and Jeremiah 33:21. Its function in the sequence is to identify the promised seed specifically as a royal descendant of Abraham through David.
parallelsWithAbraham: God promises both "a great name" (Gen. 12:2; 2 Sam. 7:9).
In the future both will conquer their enemies (Gen. 22:17; 2 Sam. 7:11; cf. Ps. 89:23).
Both have a special divine-human relationship (Gen. 17:7-8; 2 Sam. 7:24; cf. Ps. 89:26).
A special line of "seed" perpetuates both of their names (Gen. 21:12; 2 Sam. 7:12-16).
The descendants of both must keep God's laws (Gen. 18:19; 2 Sam. 7:14; cf. Pss. 89:30-32; 132:12).
The offspring of both would mediate international blessing (Gen. 22:18; Ps. 72:17).

covenants.name: New covenant
covenants.description: The new covenant, explicit at Jeremiah 31:31 and alluded to throughout Scripture. Jeremiah speaks of internalised Torah and Ezekiel of spiritual transformation, both reaching for the covenant formula "I will be their God, and they will be my people". Isaiah ties an everlasting covenant of peace to the Servant, and it is both inclusive and exclusive. Jesus ratifies it through his blood, bringing the forgiveness of sins and the eschatological blessings promised to God's people.
